extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners learning enumerative combinatorics (advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles, techniques and standards for proving counting identities and constructing combinatorial proofs (bijections, generating functions, stars-and-bars, recurrences) in enumerative combinatorics. Focuses on producing valid combinatorial arguments and on methods to derive closed forms and generating functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial proof vs non-combinatorial proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A combinatorial (or bijective) proof constructs a direct counting or bijection between combinatorial sets; a non-combinatorial proof uses algebraic/analytic manipulations (e.g., generating functions) to obtain the same numeric answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combinatorial proofs are often shorter and make the reason for a simple answer transparent; some arguments that look non-combinatorial to the inexperienced can be converted into combinatorial proofs using standard techniques. Use combinatorial proofs when they reveal structural reasons behind formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat against circular bijection proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Caveat: any proof that θ is bijective must not use a priori the fact that #S_kn = #T_kn!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proving a bijection, do not rely on pre-known cardinality equalities of the two sets being linked; construct explicit inverse or otherwise show injectivity/surjectivity combinatorially to avoid circular reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of generating functions (including exponential GFs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate counting sequences into generating functions (ordinary or exponential), e.g., define F_k(x)=sum_{n>=0} f(k,n) x^n/n! for labelled combinatorial classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generating functions can produce compact derivations and identities (and unify specializations) but may be less illuminating combinatorially; sometimes it is easier to work with the most number of variables (multivariate) then specialize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of elements principle (product counts)
rubrics_metrics.description: If different elements of the ground set behave independently with respect to the structure being counted, the total count factors as a product of independent choices (leading to exponentiation or product formulas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify independent decisions per element to obtain product formulas (e.g., each element has the same set of allowed choices, so total = (choices)^{#elements}). This often explains simple closed forms like (2^k-1)^n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditioning / summing over intersection (casewise counting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count by conditioning on an auxiliary parameter (e.g., let X1∩...∩Xk = T with |T|=i) and sum over all possible values of that parameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard casework reduces a complicated count to a sum of simpler counts; combine with combinatorial enumeration of each case to obtain the total.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristic vector bijection for subsets
rubrics_metrics.description: Map each subset T of an n-set S to its characteristic vector (ε1,...,εn) with εi in {0,1}, yielding a bijection between 2^S and {0,1}^n and proving #2^S = 2^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit, elementwise encodings to produce clean bijections between combinatorial objects and familiar algebraic objects (vectors, words).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearing the denominator (count ordered structures then divide)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a formula has a factorial denominator (e.g., n choose k = n!/k!(n-k)!), count a related ordered structure N(n,k) (choose k-subset then order it) so that N(n,k)=k! * (desired count), derive N(n,k) directly and divide by k!. (Described as 'clearing the denominator'.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technique transforms a counting-with-symmetry problem into one without symmetry, making the numerator easy to count; be explicit about the symmetry factor (k!).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multivariate-to-univariate specialization in generating functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Work with a refined multivariate generating function (one variable per combinatorial feature) and then specialize all variables to a single variable to obtain ordinary identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refined (more variables) formulas are often more transparent and their specializations follow automatically; use this to derive multiple identities from one general GF.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stars-and-bars / balls-into-boxes method for compositions and multisets
rubrics_metrics.description: Model weak compositions, multisets, or combinations with repetition as arrangements of dots and bars (k dots and n-1 bars) to obtain binomial-type counts (n+k-1 choose k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use geometric/diagrammatic stars-and-bars proofs as direct bijections between algebraic solutions and combinatorial diagrams; this yields simple closed forms for weak compositions and multisets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric/diagrammatic representation principle
rubrics_metrics.description: It is often efficacious to represent the objects being counted geometrically (diagrams, lattice paths, dots-and-bars) to reveal structure and facilitate bijections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw diagrams (lattice paths, dots with bars, digraphs) to visualize bijections and to build combinatorial arguments; diagrams often suggest natural bijections or product decompositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compression technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Technique of compression: convert strictly increasing sequences to weakly increasing sequences (or vice versa) by a simple index shift (e.g., ai = bi + i) to build bijections between k-multisets and k-subsets of a larger set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this systematic index-shifting trick to relate multisets/combinations-with-repetition to ordinary subsets, yielding closed formulas like (n+k-1 choose k).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multinomial / categorical interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret multinomial coefficients as the number of ways to assign each element of an n-set to m labelled categories with prescribed counts (or permutations of a multiset).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the balls-into-boxes viewpoint or view permutations of multisets to derive the formula n!/(a1!...am!) and to reduce problems to binomial coefficients via sequential choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lattice path interpretation of binomial/multinomial coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret binomial and multinomial coefficients as counts of lattice paths with unit coordinate steps (e.g., number of paths from origin to (a1,...,ad) with steps e1,...,ed equals a multinomial coefficient).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate combinatorial assignments into lattice path counting to exploit geometric intuition and known path-counting formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple representations of permutations (words, cycles, digraphs, inversion tables, codes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Permutations can be represented in many combinatorial ways—words (linear orderings), disjoint cycle notation, digraphs, inversion tables, or codes—and different representations illuminate different statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the representation best suited to the problem: cycles for cycle-structure counts, inversion tables for q-analogues of inversions, digraphs for graphical intuition, words for left-to-right maxima.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard cycle representation and fundamental bijection
rubrics_metrics.description: Write each cycle with its largest element first and order cycles by increasing largest element; erase parentheses to obtain a permutation word. The resulting map is a bijection relating number of cycles to number of left-to-right maxima.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the standard-cycle-to-word bijection (the fundamental bijection) to translate statements about cycles into statements about left-to-right maxima and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cycle index / cycle indicator and the exponential formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the cycle index Zn(t1,...,tn) = (1/n!) sum_{w in S_n} t^{type(w)}; the generating function sum_{n>=0} Z_n x^n equals exp(sum_{i>=1} t_i x^i / i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the cycle index and its exponential GF expansion to extract counts of permutations with restricted cycle lengths or to derive distributional results about cycle structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computing expectations via differentiation of GFs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use differentiation of generating functions with respect to marking variables to compute expected values of combinatorial statistics (e.g., expected number of k-cycles obtained by ∂/∂t_k at t_i=1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark the statistic of interest by introducing a parameter into the cycle index or GF, differentiate, then specialize parameters to 1 to obtain expected counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial recurrence via insertion (element n)
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive recurrences (e.g., for signless Stirling numbers c(n,k)) by considering where the element n is placed: either inserted into an existing cycle or forms a singleton, yielding c(n,k) = (n-1)c(n-1,k) + c(n-1,k-1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use constructive insertion/deletion of a distinguished element combined with case analysis to obtain clean combinatorial recurrences and base conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bijection from bounded integer sequences to permutations (constructive algorithms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct explicit bijections between integer sequences with bounded entries (e.g., inversion tables or the sequences used in the fourth proof of Proposition 1.3.7) and permutations by inserting elements according to the sequence entries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an explicit constructive algorithm (insert element n with prescribed number of preceding/left elements or into cycle determined by labels) and show invertibility to establish bijection; this technique yields enumerative identities and q-analogues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion table / code representation and q-analogues
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent permutations by inversion tables I(w)=(a1,...,an) with 0<=a_i<=n-i; inv(w)=sum a_i. Summing q^{inv(w)} over S_n factors as product_{i=1}^n (1+q+...+q^{i-1}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the inversion-table bijection to derive q-analog generating functions for inversion statistics (product formula), and to count permutations by inversions combinatorially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double counting (count the same set two ways)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count a combinatorial set in two different natural ways (e.g., count N(n,k) by choosing an ordered k-tuple vs choosing sequence of k distinct elements) and equate the expressions to derive identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply double counting whenever symmetry or multiple natural constructions exist; this is the basis for many binomial/multinomial identities and for deriving formulas like binomial coefficients.
